opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think one of the biggest opportunities is moving beyond the idea that a single mutation tells us everything we need to know. Genetic precision medicine has made real progress. We can sequence a tumor, find an actionable mutation, and match a patient to a targeted therapy. But in practice, many patients don't have a clear actionable target, and even when they do, response varies a lot. Two patients with the same mutation can have very different outcomes.

That's where I think machine learning can help, by integrating many kinds of data that we've historically looked at in isolation. The genomic profile is one piece. We also have medical imaging, pathology slides, lab values, treatment history, and clinical notes. My own work has focused a lot on imaging, using quantitative features from CT scans, sometimes called radiomics, to characterize tumors in ways the human eye can't. A tumor isn't uniform. There's heterogeneity in its texture and structure, and that may reflect underlying biology. Imaging is non-invasive and repeatable, so if we can link imaging patterns to genomic and molecular characteristics, we may be able to track how a tumor changes over time without repeated biopsies.

So the opportunity is really in building models that combine these data streams to predict who will respond to which treatment, who is at risk of recurrence, and how aggressive a disease is likely to be. That gets us closer to precision medicine that's about the whole patient and the whole tumor, not just one gene.

There are real challenges, of course. Cancer datasets are often small, especially for rarer cancers, and data is siloed across institutions with privacy constraints. Models trained at one hospital don't always generalize to another, because scanners, protocols, and patient populations differ. And clinicians rightly want to understand why a model makes a recommendation before acting on it. So I think progress will depend as much on data sharing, approaches like federated learning, and interpretability as on new algorithms. But the potential is enormous: helping oncologists make better-informed decisions earlier, and sparing patients treatments that are unlikely to work for them.

r001.rationale: It describes matching targeted therapy to an actionable mutation and says machine learning can move beyond relying on a single mutation.

r002.rationale: It proposes combining genomic data with imaging and other data, but does not clearly identify analyzing multiple tumor genetic variables together as the opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that genetics is only one piece of the picture. When a patient comes in with cancer, we sequence the tumor, we find a mutation, and we match it to a drug if one exists. That works for a fraction of patients. But for everyone else, and really even for those patients, the genetic profile alone doesn't tell you how the disease is going to behave or how that person is going to respond to treatment.

What we actually have on every single patient is imaging. CT scans, MRIs, the pathology slides from surgery. That data is collected routinely, it's sitting in hospital archives, and historically a radiologist or pathologist looks at it, writes a report, and the rest of the information in those images is never used. The opportunity for machine learning is to go back into that imaging and extract features that a human eye can't quantify. The texture of a tumor, its heterogeneity, how it relates to the surrounding tissue. And then we ask whether those features correlate with the underlying biology, with the mutations we care about, with how the patient actually did.

So in my lab, a lot of our work is on linking imaging to genomics. Can we predict from a CT scan that a liver metastasis carries a particular mutation? Can we tell before surgery which patients are going to recur early, so maybe they get chemotherapy first instead? That's precision medicine in a broader sense. You're using all the data you have on a patient, not just the sequencing, and imaging is cheap, non-invasive, and you can repeat it over time. Biopsies you can't.

The other thing I'd say is that precision medicine right now is mostly about matching a drug to a target. But the harder, more valuable question is often prognosis. Who needs aggressive treatment and who doesn't? Overtreatment is a real harm. If machine learning can help us say with confidence that this patient has a low-risk disease, that changes their life as much as finding a targetable mutation does. And I think models that integrate imaging, pathology, genomics, and clinical history together are where we'll get there. No single data type is going to do it alone.

r001.rationale: The response describes sequencing a tumor, finding a mutation, and matching that mutation to a drug, communicating treatment decisions based on individual genetic markers.

r002.rationale: The response proposes linking or integrating genomics with imaging, pathology, and clinical history, but does not identify multivariable analysis of tumor genetic data as an opportunity.

astra-6.text:
One opportunity is to use machine learning to connect a tumor’s genetic profile with what we see in medical images and with how a patient responds to treatment. A genetic mutation can suggest a therapy, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us whether that therapy will work for a particular patient. By bringing those different sources of information together, we may be able to make more useful predictions about treatment response.

The key is making sure those predictions hold up in new patients and actually help clinicians make decisions. That’s where the promise of precision medicine becomes meaningful: helping choose the right treatment for the person in front of you.

r001.rationale: It says a mutation can suggest a therapy, but does not state that treatment decisions often rely on individual tumor genetic markers considered one at a time.

r002.rationale: It proposes combining a genetic profile with imaging and treatment response, but does not identify multivariable analysis of tumor genetic data as the opportunity.

sol-6.1.text:
I see a real opportunity in connecting the genetic information we get from a tumor with the information we already collect during routine care, particularly medical images. A biopsy samples one small part of a tumor, while imaging gives us a broader view of the disease. Machine learning could help us connect those different perspectives to better understand why patients respond differently to treatment.

The goal is to help clinicians choose the right treatment for an individual patient. But we need to show that these models work across different hospitals and patient populations, and that using them actually improves care.

r001.rationale: The response discusses connecting tumor genetic information with medical images, but does not say treatment decisions commonly consider individual tumor genetic markers one at a time.

r002.rationale: The response proposes combining genetic information with imaging, but does not identify multivariable analysis of tumor genetic data as the opportunity.
